results.text:
## Overview

The Lexsi - AI Safety and Alignment Hackathon is organized by Lexsi Labs, in partnership with Cohere Labs and Hugging Face, to bring Lexsi Labs' open-source tools into the hands of builders working on real alignment, safety, data, interpretability, and tabular-modeling problems.

Lexsi Labs is a Frontier Model Science lab producing research in interpretability, alignment, and tabular foundational models, deployed at enterprise scale. Lexsi Labs holds the #1 Tabular Foundational Model on Enterprise Datasets, with labs in Mumbai, Paris, and London.

### GOAL OF THE HACKATHON

The goal is to bring together a global community of builders to explore and extend a set of open-source post-training and interpretability toolkits. The hackathon is designed to make Lexsi Labs' open-source model-lifecycle stack public, and to gather real-world feedback and feature requests from builders to improve it further.

Above all, the hackathon is about promoting AI safety and alignment: getting more builders hands-on with red teaming, safety repair, interpretability and evaluation, so that making models safer and better aligned becomes a routine part of how they are post-trained and shipped. Projects, datasets and findings stay open, so the wider community can build on them.

For participants, the goal is to chain the stack into a real pipeline and show, with before-and-after metrics, that a small open-weights model becomes meaningfully better, safer or more reliable for a real use case.

### HACKATHON HIGHLIGHTS

* Runs fully online from Nov 1 to Nov 21, 2026: submit by Nov 14, with Demo Day on Nov 22.
* Kickoff event on Oct 31: an introduction to the open-source stack, its key features and functionality.
* Build with the open-source stack: AlignTune, AgentTune, AuditKIT, CuratorKIT, CircuitKIT, and SafeTune.
* Three tracks: Fine-tuning and Data Curation, AI Red Teaming, Safety and Alignment, and Agentic Fine-tuning.
* Use dense, open-weights LLMs from Cohere Labs.
* Host your models, adapters, logs, and datasets on Hugging Face.
* Up to 20 shortlisted teams, announced by Nov 16, get until Nov 21 to prove their thesis, then present a live demo to the judges on Demo Day, Nov 22.
* Interview opportunities for standout candidates, for DevRel / Research Internship roles or Research Scientist / Engineer roles.

### WHO SHOULD ATTEND

This hackathon is open to builders from across the AI ecosystem, whether you're just getting started with post-training or already working on frontier model problems, including:

* Undergraduates and beginners interested in AI safety and alignment
* Students and open-source contributors
* AI / ML Engineers
* Researchers working on alignment, safety, and interpretability
* LLM and fine-tuning practitioners
* Data engineers and data scientists, including tabular-modeling practitioners
* Red teamers and AI safety enthusiasts
* Agent and tool-use builders

### OUR OPEN SOURCE STACK

* AlignTune: A modular toolkit for post-training LLMs, with 20+ algorithms and any backend (TRL, Unsloth and more) behind one unified API.
* CuratorKIT: A data-curation and synthetic-data pipeline that turns raw documents or datasets into quality-gated, deduplicated, hallucination-checked training data.
* AuditKIT: An evaluation suite with a collection of benchmarks, metrics and diagnosis.
* SafeTune: A library for auditing and repairing safety drift in fine-tuned LLMs, from train-time hardening to weight-space fixes and inference-time steering.
* CircuitKIT: A mechanistic-interpretability framework for discovering, evaluating and intervening on circuits inside transformer models.
* AgentTune: A library for post-training agents to make tool calls more accurate, efficient and reliable.

For the full list, check out our GitHub.

## Schedule

The hackathon is online. The kickoff event and demo day are in-person, with an online option for those who can't travel. Kickoff venue: Polaris School of Technology, Bengaluru.

### Registration

Registration opens on Oct 12 and closes on Nov 5.

### Kickoff Event

An introduction to the open-source stack, its key features and functionality.

Held in-person, with an online option for those who can't travel.

### Hackathon

The hackathon runs fully online across all three tracks: Fine-tuning and Data Curation, AI Red Teaming, Safety and Alignment, and Agentic Fine-tuning.

Build your project and submit it by end of day on Nov 14.

### Submission Deadline

All submissions are due by end of day on Nov 14. Late or incomplete submissions may not be considered.

### Demo Day Teams Announced

Judging is complete, and up to 20 teams are informed that they are through to Demo Day.

### Demo Day

Shortlisted teams get Nov 16 – 21 to prove their thesis, then present a live demo, after which the judges will discuss and decide the final winners.

Held in-person, with an online option for those who can't travel.

## Structure

How the hackathon runs, from registration to Demo Day.

### Register

Registration opens on Oct 12 and closes on Nov 5, so teams can still join after the hackathon starts.

### Build and submit Nov 1 – 14

Submissions are due by end of day on Nov 14.

Registered teams that also join our Discord get $20 in HF credits to use on ZeroGPU or other GPU instances, for up to 800 teams.

Google Colab and Kaggle also give generous free GPU quotas, which can be enough for the Tiny Aya models.

### Judging Nov 15 – 16

Judges from across industry and academia score every submission and shortlist up to 20 teams for Demo Day. When teams are close, the judges discuss them together before deciding. Demo Day teams are informed by Nov 16.

### Prove your thesis Nov 16 – 21

Shortlisted teams get until Nov 21 to prove their thesis before Demo Day, plus a further $200 in HF credits to improve and polish their submission and artifacts, or to run any extra experiments they need.

### Demo Day and final judging Nov 22

Demo Day teams present their work live, in person or online. A panel of judges from the organizing and partner organizations, along with industry experts, then reviews every finalist and decides the final winners and prizes.

### About the credits

* Emails about credits go to the team lead, using the details from the submission form.
* Only teams whose Hugging Face usernames match the ones in the registration form are eligible for credits.
* Hugging Face may ask you to link a payment method to redeem the coupon.
* The $20 coupon works for the first 800 teams that redeem it. After that, it may stop working.
* Credits expire 30 days after you redeem them.

## Tracks

We strongly recommend focusing on one preferred track, but you are permitted to submit more than one. In case more than one gets submitted, the final submission prior to submission deadline will be the only one that will be considered.

You are free to explore other ideas that fall within the scope of the rules, but we recommend validating the idea with the team by raising a Discord ticket via the #report-issues channel.

Raise a ticket on Discord

### Fine-tuning and Data Curation

curate / generate training data

post-train the model

evaluate and benchmark the result

#### AlignTune

A modular toolkit for post-training of LLMs, with any of the 20+ algorithms and any backend (TRL/Unsloth/etc..) behind a single unified API, compatible with any open-source model.

#### CuratorKIT

A data-curation and synthetic-data-generation pipeline for LLM post-training, ingesting raw documents or datasets and producing quality-gated, deduplicated, hallucination-checked training data in trainer-ready formats.

#### Problem statements

1. Domain assistants for regulated industries: Adapt a model to a regulated domain such as banking, insurance, legal or healthcare, where answers must follow policy and stay accurate.
2. Replacing a closed-model API: Take a high-volume business task that is usually sent to a large closed model (classification, extraction, summarisation, drafting) and fine-tune a small open model to match it at a fraction of the cost.
3. Grounded answers and fewer hallucinations: Build a training set from an organisation's own documents (manuals, policies, contracts, research) and train a model that answers only from them. It should say so when the answer is not there and make measurably fewer unsupported or false claims.
4. Low-resource and multilingual languages: Improve a model for underserved languages, dialects or code-mixed text in a public-facing setting such as education, public services, agriculture or healthcare.
5. Structured output and extraction: Turn unstructured text (forms, invoices, reports, clinical notes, support tickets) into reliable structured data that passes schema validation.
6. Reasoning with verifiable answers: Improve step-by-step reasoning in areas where answers can be checked automatically, such as maths, financial calculations, code or logic, using reward-based training.
7. Preference and style alignment: Align a model with an organisation's quality bar or house style (customer communication, technical writing, feedback on student work) using preference data.
8. Data-scarce domains: Where little real data exists, generate, verify and filter synthetic training data, and show that curation measurably beats training on raw generated data.
9. Long documents: Fine-tune for summarising and reasoning over long documents such as filings, contracts, transcripts or research papers through multi-stage fine tuning.

### AI Red Teaming, Safety and Alignment

build a safety-focused dataset

audit and repair safety drift

locate and intervene on the underlying circuits

evaluate the hardened model

#### SafeTune

A library for auditing and repairing safety drift in fine-tuned LLMs, covering train-time hardening, weight-space interventions, and inference-time steering, plus built-in tools to locate safety-relevant circuits and neurons.

#### CuratorKIT

A data-curation and synthetic-data-generation pipeline for LLM post-training, ingesting raw documents or datasets and producing quality-gated, deduplicated, hallucination-checked training data in trainer-ready formats.

#### CircuitKIT

A mechanistic-interpretability framework for discovering, evaluating, and intervening on circuits inside transformer-based models, including pruning, quantization, knowledge editing, and circuit-restricted fine-tuning.

#### Problem statements

##### Track 2a: AI Safety and Red Teaming

1. Red-teaming and robustness evaluation: Attack a hardened model with jailbreaks, prompt injection, encoding tricks, best-of-N sampling and weight-space attacks such as abliteration, and report robustness alongside over-refusal.
2. Adversarial and safety evaluation sets: Build an adversarial or safety benchmark for a specific domain, language or risk area, with clear labels and scoring, and use it to measure how current open models hold up. The deliverable can be the dataset and a report.
3. Multi-turn audits: Audit a model or agent across long, multi-turn conversations for attacks a single prompt would not catch, such as prompt injection hidden in tools or documents, gradual jailbreaks and requests for cyber-attack help. Report what broke and in which turn, with reproducible transcripts.
4. Multilingual and code-mixed safety: Test whether safety holds across languages and mixed-language prompts, then close the gaps you find.

##### Track 2b: AI Safety and Correction

5. Safety-preserving fine-tuning: Fine-tune a model for a useful domain task with a safety-hardening method, and show safety holds compared with plain fine-tuning.
6. Repairing safety drift without retraining: Take a model whose safety degraded after fine-tuning and restore it with weight-space methods (safety patching, merging, projection) while keeping task performance.
7. Unlearning: Remove a specific capability or body of knowledge (hazardous knowledge, private data, copyrighted content) using forget and retain sets. Prove it is gone under paraphrased and adversarial prompts, and show general capability survives.
8. Inference-time safety steering: Block harmful requests with activation steering (refusal directions, contrastive or conditional steering) or safety-aware decoding, with no retraining, while keeping over-refusal of harmless requests low.
9. Locating where safety lives: Find the circuits, neurons or directions responsible for refusal or for a harmful behaviour, and use them to make a targeted fix.
10. Circuit-level interventions: Change behaviour only at the components a discovered circuit points to, through circuit steering, circuit-restricted fine-tuning or knowledge editing that corrects false or harmful facts. Verify nothing else broke.
11. Safety-aware compression: Compress a model with circuit-aware mixed-precision quantization or pruning, and show its safety behaviour survives the compression.
12. Tamper resistance: Make safety survive later harmful fine-tuning by someone else, and demonstrate it with attack fine-tunes.
13. Hallucination detection and abstention: Train probes on the model's internal activations to flag likely hallucinations, and wire them in so the model abstains or triggers retrieval when a probe fires. Show fewer wrong answers while it still answers most questions.

### Agentic Fine-tuning

post-train the agent for reliable tool use

evaluate tool-call accuracy and reliability

#### AgentTune

A library for post-training agents for better tool calls, syntax, and efficiency to reduce redundant or incorrect tool calls and to improve reliability.

#### Problem statements

1. Reliable tool calling: Train an agent with reinforcement learning on real tool-calling rollouts to choose the right tool, pass well-formed arguments and call tools in the right order.
2. Efficient trajectories: Cut redundant, looping or failed tool calls and the number of steps per task, without lowering the success rate.
3. Agentic distillation: Distill a stronger teacher's agent trajectories into a small student model that is cheap to run or runs locally.
4. Fine-tuning for retrieval-augmented generation: Train a model that decides when and what to retrieve, grounds its answers in the retrieved text and ignores distracting documents.
5. Synthetic multi-hop training data: Turn a document corpus into grounded, difficulty-graded multi-hop questions and use them to train a research or search agent.
6. Data and database agents: Train an agent that answers business questions by querying databases or APIs (finance, operations, analytics), rewarded on verified results.
7. Business workflow and decision agents: Automate a multi-step process with rules and approvals, such as claims handling, KYC checks, ticket triage or compliance review, with a full audit trail.
8. Self-healing agents: Detect failing runs, classify why they failed, generate corrective training examples, retrain, and gate redeployment on measured accuracy.
9. Reward design and reward-hacking defences: Design rewards (process rewards, LLM judges, groundedness checks) that raise real task success without being gamed.

## Eligibility

The Lexsi - AI Safety and Alignment Hackathon is open to builders worldwide from across the AI ecosystem, whether you're just getting started with post-training or already working on frontier model problems, including:

* Undergraduates and beginners interested in AI safety and alignment
* Students and open-source contributors
* AI / ML Engineers
* Researchers working on alignment, safety, and interpretability
* LLM and fine-tuning practitioners
* Data engineers and data scientists, including tabular-modeling practitioners
* Red teamers and AI safety enthusiasts
* Agent and tool-use builders

Participation is team-based, with teams of 1 to 3 members, and each participant can only participate through one team. The hackathon runs fully online, and all participants must complete their registration before registration closes on Nov 5.

## Rules

### 1. Team Formation

* Teams may consist of 1 to 3 members.
* Each participant can only participate through one team.
* Looking for teammates? Find them in the #find-teammates channel on our Discord server.
* At least one member of each team should join the Discord server to get updates and announcements.

### 2. Project Requirements

* Projects must be developed during the hackathon.
* All submissions must chain together repos from their track into a real pipeline.
* Minimum: at least 2 repos from the track, used together (except Track 3).
* Preferred: 3 or more repos from the track, used together.

### 3. Models

* Use a dense, open-weights LLM from Cohere Labs:

### 4. Hugging Face Artifacts

* Host all artifacts created on Hugging Face:
  + Models
  + Adapters
  + Logs
  + Datasets

### 5. Submissions

* Projects must be deployed publicly (e.g. a public demo or repository link) by the submission deadline.
* Showcase before-and-after metrics (more than one metric).
* Write-up: the metrics chosen and why, the approach and rationale behind the choice of datasets, tasks, and models, and how the resulting model is meaningfully better for usage.
  + A HF Article
  + A HF Space (if relevant)
  + [Optional but preferred] An ROI comparison of a closed-source model vs. the fine-tuned/aligned smaller model — self-hosting cost vs. closed-source token billing, using a realistic sample volume, GPU runtime hours, per-hour GPU pricing, and an estimated tokens/sec throughput.
* If more than one submission is made, only the final submission prior to the submission deadline will be considered.
* Late or incomplete submissions may not be considered for evaluation.

### 6. Originality

* The contributions should be unique and your own work.
* Open-source libraries and publicly available datasets may be used where permitted.

### 7. Code of Conduct

* Treat all participants, mentors, organizers, and volunteers with respect.
* Harassment, plagiarism, or disruptive behavior may result in disqualification.

### 8. Intellectual Property

* Teams retain ownership of the solutions they develop.
* Organizers may showcase submitted projects for event and promotional purposes.

### 9. Organizer Rights

* Organizers reserve the right to modify the schedule or event rules if required.
* All decisions made by the organizers regarding the hackathon will be final.

## Submit

Submissions are due by end of day on Nov 14 (AoE). You can submit more than once; your latest submission counts.

### What you'll need

* The email you or a teammate registered with
* An abstract of your submission, under 500 words
* Your Hugging Face model collection
  + Add all models, adapters, etc. into a HF collection, with all individual repos and the collection public (un-gated).
* Your Hugging Face dataset collection
  + Add all datasets, logs, traces, benchmarks, curated or synthetic data, etc. into a HF collection, with all individual repos and the collection public.
* Your write-up or article
  + If HF articles are accessible, use them; otherwise, a GitHub repo README is also acceptable.
* Your GitHub repo (code or a set of notebooks)
  + If a repo is used, ensure the README covers reproducibility notes.
  + If notebooks were used, submit them via a GitHub repo.
* The repos and models you used, your track or tracks, and your problem statements

## Support

Our team is here to help you with any queries or concerns.

## Referral Program

Get your own link to the Lexsi - AI Safety and Alignment Hackathon and share it. Every registration that comes through your link is counted for you.

### HOW IT WORKS

* Generate your link below with your email, so we know it's yours.
* Share it with friends, classmates, communities and on your socials.
* Every registration made through your link is counted for you, even if they browse the site first or come back later.
* Points are based on the sign-ups and project submissions of the teams that registered through your link.

### TIPS TO GET MORE REFERRALS

* Print your QR code and put it up on notice boards and walls around your university or college.\*
* Post your link on LinkedIn and X.
* Share it in group chats: class, batch, lab and hostel WhatsApp, Telegram and Discord groups.
* Ask your college clubs (AI/ML, coding, ACM/IEEE chapters) to share it with their members.
* Tell your classmates and lab mates in person, and show them the QR code on your phone.

\* Only where posting is allowed. Follow your campus rules and local laws, and get permission where it's needed.

### YOUR REFERRAL LINK

Share this exact link. It's yours and stays the same.

### REWARDS

Rewards are based on the number of teams that register with your referral link and make a valid submission to the hackathon. Each milestone adds platform credits on top of the last.

Generate your referral link to track your progress here.

Credits add up: a link that brings 10 teams with valid submissions earns $5 + $10 + $20 = $35 in credits.
